Explain what is historically shared and what Wikipedia says about the status of these theories. Do not assume this single page uniquely identifies Franklin's rather than every other fluid theory. **The Britannica page's language on "redundant fluid"**

The Britannica ELECTRICITY page (Supplement to the 3rd ed., Vol. 1, ABE–IMP, 1776 scan) discusses electricity entirely in terms of a "fluid" distributed through conductors. Its key passages say:

- "bodies … when overcharged, will have the **redundant fluid** much denser near the surface than in the interior parts; and denser in all directions, bumps, projections, angles, and near the exit of oblong bodies, and … the quantity of redundant fluid, or redundant matter, will be much more nearly proportional to the [surfaces] than their quantities of matter." [bri-1776-5ed864a29d36:region-5:0]
- A figure's ordinates represent "the capable density of the fluid, were like the conductor is in his natural flame; but [others] represent the unequal densities in its different points, while in the vicinity of the overcharged figure… the redundant matter, or deficient fluids in any [portion]." [bri-1776-5ed864a29d36:image]

This treats **excess ("redundant") and deficient fluid as states of a body relative to a "natural" or neutral amount**, with charge residing on surfaces and concentrating at points and edges — language characteristic of a **one-fluid (unitary) model**, in which a single electrical fluid is present in excess or lacking.

**What it shares with Wikipedia's account of fluid theories**

Wikipedia's "Fluid theory of electricity" page describes the same fluid framework: electricity was postulated as one or more electrical fluids responsible for electrical phenomena [wiki-2586411-1317149477-7fa48999b86a]. It specifically describes Benjamin Franklin's one-fluid theory as holding that "electricity was really one fluid, which could be present in excess, or absent from a body, thus explaining its electrical charge" [wiki-2586411-1317149477-7fa48999b86a], and explains that a body shows electricity "when it held either too much, or too little of this liquid," with a neutral object containing a "normal" amount [wiki-2586411-1317149477-99bc0df3f29c]. Wikipedia also describes the competing two-fluid theory of du Fay (two liquids, one positive/vitreous and one negative/resinous) [wiki-2586411-1317149477-7fa48999b86a; wiki-2586411-1317149477-6a5f22387a19].

The shared historical substance: both treat electricity as a material-like fluid whose **excess or deficiency relative to a neutral baseline produces charge**, with the surplus fluid residing on a body's surface — the core intuition behind Franklin's one-fluid theory. The Britannica passage's "redundant fluid … denser near the surface" is essentially this one-fluid picture applied to distribution over conductors.

**What Wikipedia says about the status of these theories**

Wikipedia is explicit that these are **outdated, superseded theories**: "Fluid theories of electricity are outdated theories that postulated one or more electrical fluids which were thought to be responsible for many electrical phenomena" [wiki-2586411-1317149477-7fa48999b86a]. It notes that "although fluid theory was the predominant viewpoint for a time, it was eventually replaced by more modern theories" [wiki-2586411-1317149477-590e8957350b], and that neither du Fay's nor Franklin's theory explained magnetism — a deficiency resolved only when Ørsted and Ampère unified electricity and magnetism [wiki-2586411-1317149477-590e8957350b; wiki-2586411-1317149477-a01e492c6b41]. Wikipedia also records that the one-fluid vs. two-fluid question "was heavily debated … for a century" [wiki-2586411-1317149477-99bc0df3f29c], so the fluid framework was a live 18th-century debate, not settled doctrine.

**Caveat on identifying Franklin uniquely**

You asked not to assume this single page uniquely identifies Franklin rather than every other fluid theory. That caution is warranted: the Britannica extract never names Franklin, du Fay, one-fluid, or two-fluid theory. It simply uses "redundant fluid" / "deficient fluid" language — the generic vocabulary of 18th-century fluid electrical theory. The one-fluid reading (excess/deficiency of a single fluid relative to neutrality) is an inference from the concepts present (redundant vs. deficient fluid, surface concentration), not an identification the page itself makes. The broader fluid-theory family (one-fluid and two-fluid alike) is what the page's language participates in.

Electrorheological (ER) fluids are suspensions of extremely fine non-conducting but electrically active particles (up to 50 micrometres diameter) in an electrically insulating fluid. The apparent viscosity of these fluids changes reversibly by an order of up to 100,000 in response to an electric field. For example, a typical ER fluid can go from the consistency of a liquid to that of a gel, and back, with response times on the order of milliseconds. The effect is sometimes called the Winslow effect after its discoverer, the American inventor Willis Winslow, who obtained a US patent on the effect in 1947 and wrote an article published in 1949.

The change in apparent viscosity is dependent on the applied electric field, i.e. the potential divided by the distance between the plates. The change is not a simple change in viscosity, hence these fluids are now known as ER fluids, rather than by the older term Electro Viscous fluids. The effect is better described as an electric field dependent shear yield stress. When activated an ER fluid behaves as a Bingham plastic (a type of viscoelastic material), with a yield point which is determined by the electric field strength. After the yield point is reached, the fluid shears as a fluid, i.e. the incremental shear stress is proportional to the rate of shear (in a Newtonian fluid there is no yield point and stress is directly proportional to shear). Hence the resistance to motion of the fluid can be controlled by adjusting the applied electric field.

The Bohnenberger electrometer, developed by J. G. F. von Bohnenberger from an invention by T. G. B. Behrens, consists of a single gold leaf suspended vertically between the anode and cathode of a dry pile. Any charge imparted to the gold leaf causes it to move toward one or the other pole; thus, the sign of the charge as well as its approximate magnitude may be gauged.

Also known as "attracted disk electrometers", attraction electrometers are sensitive balances measuring the attraction between charged disks. William Snow Harris is credited with the invention of this instrument, which was further improved by Lord Kelvin.

The segments are insulated and connected diagonally in pairs. The charged aluminum sector is attracted to one pair of segments and repelled from the other. The deflection is observed by a beam of light reflected from a small mirror attached to the sector, just as in a galvanometer.
